answer: Behavioral Marble Clustering. Agents are grouped by similarity of their long-horizon action sequences; an identity whose behavior sits implausibly close to an existing cluster's centroid is flagged as a probable duplicate. Enforcement then merges or discounts the suspect identity's influence and payouts. The velvet edge is that genuine newcomers drift apart naturally, while a sybil operator must sustain distinct, costly behavioral histories per identity across the full observation window, raising marginal cost per surviving persona well above one.
